newsitem.title: LESOTHO: Lesotho calls in first S.African water royalties.
newsitem.headline: Lesotho calls in first S.African water royalties.

text.p: The first royalty payment of 100 million rand ($22 million) for the Lesotho Highlands water project will be paid to the kingdom's government by South Africa at the end of October, an official said on Wednesday.
The Lesotho Highlands Development Authority's chief executive, Makase Marumo, said the cash handover was in accordance with a water treaty signed in October 1986.

"Now that the water level of the main reservoir of the water project has reached 1,993 metres above sea level, we can send an invoice to the South African government to pay," Marumo said in a statement.

The Lesotho Highlands Water Project is a $5 billion joint venture by Lesotho and South Africa which aims to harness the tiny landlocked country's abundant water resources for the benefit of both southern African countries.

When the project -- Africa's largest construction venture -- is completed in 2020, water supply to South Africa's industrial and commercial heartland around Johannesburg will have doubled and Lesotho will generate its own electricity.

But a South African academic warned on Wednesday Lesotho's government needed to develop an economic strategy to counter its heavy reliance on the water project for income and consider the socio-economic consequences of its completion.

"It is cause for concern that Lesotho's economic development has depended heavily on the Lesotho Highlands water project," the University of Cape Town economics lecturer, Iraj Abedian, told a United Nations Development Programme meeting in Maseru.

"As the project winds down it is likely that the gross domestic product growth will decline and given a declining mining industry in South Africa, migrant remittances are also likely to decline," Abedian said.
Lesotho, surrounded by South Africa and about the size of Belgium, receives much of its foreign exchange earnings from migrant workers working in the gold mines of South Africa.
The mountainous kingdom has greatly benefited from the project in recent years.

With some of the most inaccessible terrain on the African continent over 400 km (250 miles) of roads had to be constructed from scratch or improved before main construction on the water project could start. The spillover effect has seen border posts upgraded and tourists arriving in greater numbers.
